claim: Human H3N2 influenza viruses are subject to rapid antigenic evolution which translates into frequent updates of the composition of seasonal influenza vaccines.
source: Human H3N2 influenza viruses are subject to rapid antigenic evolution which translates into frequent updates of the composition of seasonal influenza vaccines.
evidence: This is a statement about the general behavior of H3N2 viruses and vaccine policy, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The effectiveness of influenza vaccines against H3N2-associated disease is suboptimal despite frequent updates.
source: Despite these updates, the effectiveness of influenza vaccines against H3N2-associated disease is suboptimal.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about H3N2 vaccine effectiveness.

claim: Seasonal influenza vaccines primarily induce hemagglutinin-specific antibody responses.
source: Seasonal influenza vaccines primarily induce hemagglutinin-specific antibody responses.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about current influenza vaccine mechanisms.

claim: Antibodies directed against influenza neuraminidase (NA) also contribute to protection.
source: However, antibodies directed against influenza neuraminidase (NA) also contribute to protection.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge about NA antibodies.

claim: At least four antigenic groups can be distinguished in the N2 NAs derived from human H3N2 viruses that circulated between 2009 and 2017.
source: This assessment allowed us to distinguish at least four antigenic groups in the N2 NAs derived from human H3N2 viruses that circulated between 2009 and 2017.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental NAI data and clustering analysis.

claim: The amino acid residues in N2 NA that have a major impact on susceptibility to NAI by immune sera are in proximity of the catalytic site.
source: Computational analysis further revealed that the amino acid residues in N2 NA that have a major impact on susceptibility to NAI by immune sera are in proximity of the catalytic site.
evidence: This finding is based on computational analysis of the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: A machine learning method was developed that allowed to accurately predict the impact of mutations that are present in the N2 NA panel on NAI.
source: Finally, a machine learning method was developed that allowed to accurately predict the impact of mutations that are present in our N2 NA panel on NAI.
evidence: This is a methodological finding of the study based on the random forest modeling approach.

claim: Neuraminidase (NA) and hemagglutinin (HA) constitute the two major antigenic proteins at the surface of influenza A and B virions.
source: Neuraminidase (NA) and hemagglutinin (HA) constitute the two major antigenic proteins at the surface of influenza A and B virions (Uyeki et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Uyeki et al., 2022.

claim: HA mediates binding to sialic acids and membrane fusion.
source: While HA mediates binding to sialic acids and membrane fusion, NA catalyses the removal of sialic acid residues from sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HA function.

claim: NA catalyses the removal of sialic acid residues from sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids.
source: While HA mediates binding to sialic acids and membrane fusion, NA catalyses the removal of sialic acid residues from sialylated glycoproteins and glycolipids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NA enzymatic function.

claim: The complementary role of HA and NA enables influenza virions to penetrate the mucus barrier that lines the respiratory epithelium.
source: This complementary role of HA and NA enables influenza virions to penetrate the mucus barrier that lines the respiratory epithelium and newly formed virions to be released from the infected cell (de Vries et al., 2020; Matrosovich et al., 2004; Palese et al., 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to de Vries et al., 2020; Matrosovich et al., 2004; Palese et al., 1974.

claim: The complementary role of HA and NA enables newly formed virions to be released from the infected cell.
source: This complementary role of HA and NA enables influenza virions to penetrate the mucus barrier that lines the respiratory epithelium and newly formed virions to be released from the infected cell (de Vries et al., 2020; Matrosovich et al., 2004; Palese et al., 1974).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to de Vries et al., 2020; Matrosovich et al., 2004; Palese et al., 1974.

claim: Immunity against influenza is associated with the presence of anti-HA antibodies in serum, as determined by a hemagglutination inhibition assay.
source: Immunity against influenza is associated with the presence of anti-HA antibodies in serum, as determined by a hemagglutination inhibition assay.
evidence: This is established knowledge about influenza immunity assessment.

claim: The composition of licensed influenza vaccines is primarily focused on the antigenic characteristics of HA as the protective vaccine antigen.
source: In line with this, the composition of licensed influenza vaccines is primarily focused on the antigenic characteristics of HA as the protective vaccine antigen (Cox, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cox, 2013.

claim: Multiple studies have underscored the protective potential of anti-NA immune responses as determined by NA inhibition (NAI) assays.
source: Multiple studies, however, have underscored the protective potential of anti-NA immune responses as determined by NA inhibition (NAI) assays (Couch et al., 2013; Maier et al., 2020; Memoli et al., 2016; Monto and Kendal, 1973; Monto et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations: Couch et al., 2013; Maier et al., 2020; Memoli et al., 2016; Monto and Kendal, 1973; Monto et al., 2015; Ng et al., 2019; Weiss et al., 2020.

claim: Pre-existing anti-N2 immunity induced by prior exposure to H2N2 viruses that circulated in the population from 1957 to 1968 tempered the impact of the H3N2 pandemic virus that emerged in 1968.
source: There is also evidence that pre-existing anti-N2 immunity induced by prior exposure to H2N2 viruses that circulated in the population from 1957 to 1968 tempered the impact of the H3N2 pandemic virus that emerged in 1968 (Eickhoff and Meiklejohn, 1969; Jester et al., 2020; Monto and Kendal, 1973; Viboud et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Eickhoff and Meiklejohn, 1969; Jester et al., 2020; Monto and Kendal, 1973; Viboud et al., 2005.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of NA activity is a well-established therapeutic strategy to try to reduce influenza severity and duration.
source: Further, the pharmacological inhibition of NA activity is a well-established therapeutic strategy to try to reduce influenza severity and duration (Leneva et al., 2000; Yen et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Leneva et al., 2000; Yen et al., 2005.

claim: Antibodies with NAI activity can protect against influenza virus infection in pre-clinical models.
source: In addition, antibodies with NAI activity can protect against influenza virus infection in pre-clinical models (Chen et al., 2018; Deroo et al., 1996; Rosu et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2018; Wohlbold et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018; Deroo et al., 1996; Rosu et al., 2022; Wan et al., 2018; Wohlbold et al., 2017.

claim: Human H3N2 viruses have been evolving faster than the co-circulating H1N1 and influenza B viruses since its appearance in 1968.
source: Since its appearance in 1968, human H3N2 viruses have been evolving faster than the co-circulating H1N1 and influenza B viruses (Bedford et al., 2014; Potter et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bedford et al., 2014; Potter et al., 2019.

claim: The effectiveness of influenza vaccines against H3N2-associated disease ranges between 5% and 39%, which is lower than the effectiveness against H1N1 and influenza B.
source: The overall influenza virus vaccine effectiveness varies between seasons and, despite frequent updates of the H3N2 HA component, the effectiveness of influenza vaccines against H3N2-associated disease ranges between 5% and 39%, which is lower than the effectiveness against H1N1 and influenza B (Belongia et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Belongia et al., 2016.

claim: The use of NA as a complementary vaccine antigen might improve influenza vaccine effectiveness by compensating for HA-based antigenic mismatches in circulating influenza virus strains.
source: In this context the use of NA as a complementary vaccine antigen might improve influenza vaccine effectiveness, e.g., by compensating for HA-based antigenic mismatches in circulating influenza virus strains (Krammer et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Krammer et al., 2018 and represents a hypothesis about potential vaccine improvement.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses of HA and NA genes of human H3N2 viruses revealed the asynchronous evolution of the two proteins.
source: Phylogenetic analyses of HA and NA genes of human H3N2 viruses revealed the asynchronous evolution of the two proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about H3N2 evolution.

claim: The evolutionary rate as determined by the accumulation of mutations over time is estimated to be 1.5 times lower for NA than for HA.
source: In addition, the evolutionary rate as determined by the accumulation of mutations over time is estimated to be 1.5 times lower for NA than for HA (Westgeest et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Westgeest et al., 2012.

claim: A comprehensive insight in the antigenic breadth and evolution of the H3N2 NA antigen is lacking.
source: Despite the strong evidence that immune responses directed against NA can contribute to protection against influenza, a comprehensive insight in the antigenic breadth and evolution of the H3N2 NA antigen is lacking (Nachbagauer et al., 2017; Rajendran et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2004; Westgeest et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nachbagauer et al., 2017; Rajendran et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2004; Westgeest et al., 2012.

claim: 43 H3N2 NA protein sequences were selected from viruses isolated between 2009 and 2017 via GISAID.
source: We first selected 43 H3N2 NA protein sequences obtained via GISAID, derived from viruses that were isolated between 2009 and 2017 (Elbe and Buckland-Merrett, 2017).
evidence: This describes the data collection method used in the study.

claim: Hierarchical clustering with minimax linkage was employed to ensure the set was representative of overall protein sequence diversity.
source: Hierarchical clustering with minimax linkage was employed to ensure the set was representative of overall protein sequence diversity (Bien and Tibshirani, 2011).
evidence: This describes the computational method used in the study, supported by citation to Bien and Tibshirani, 2011.

claim: 43 recombinant H1N2 viruses were generated that carried the internal and HA genes from PR8 virus and the NA genes of the selected H3N2 viruses.
source: Next, 43 recombinant H1N2 viruses were generated that carried the internal and HA genes from PR8 virus and the NA genes of the selected H3N2 viruses.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Tetrabrachion-stabilised recombinant N2 NA proteins were produced in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells and purified, and are referred to as NACHOs.
source: In addition, the corresponding tetrabrachion-stabilised recombinant N2 NA proteins were produced in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells and purified, and are referred to as NACHOs (Catani et al., 2022).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study, with citation to Catani et al., 2022.

claim: All purified NACHOs were tetrameric based on SEC-MALS analysis.
source: All purified NACHOs were tetrameric based on SEC-MALS analysis.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: The NACHOs were active with a specific activity ranging from 0.27 to 27.48 nmole/min/µg, indicating correct folding and assembly of the NA head domains.
source: The NACHOs were active with a specific activity ranging from 0.27 to 27.48 nmole/min/µg, indicating correct folding and assembly of the NA head domains (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study with inference about protein structure.

claim: Immune sera against all 43 H3N2-derived NAs were generated in pairs of ferrets by a primary infection with the respective H1N2 reassortant viruses.
source: Immune sera against all 43 H3N2-derived NAs were generated in pairs of ferrets by a primary infection with the respective H1N2 reassortant viruses.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: On day 28 after primary infection, all animals were boosted by intramuscular injection of homologous NACHO, except for the ferrets that had been primed by infection with A/Stockholm/15/2014 and A/Estonia/91621/2015, which were re-inoculated with the same respective H1N2 reassortant viruses.
source: On day 28 after primary infection, all animals were boosted by intramuscular injection of homologous NACHO, except for the ferrets that had been primed by infection with A/Stockholm/15/2014 and A/Estonia/91621/2015, which were re-inoculated with the same respective H1N2 reassortant viruses.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Blood samples were taken from the ferrets on days 14 and 42 after (primary) infection.
source: Blood samples were taken from the ferrets on days 14 and 42 after (primary) infection (Figure 1a; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol, with reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Priming by H1N2 infection resulted in seroconversion against the respective immobilised homologous NACHOs.
source: Priming by H1N2 infection resulted in seroconversion against the respective immobilised homologous NACHOs (Figure 1b; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Subsequent immunisation with recombinant NACHOs boosted the NACHO-specific IgG titers in day 42 serum samples.
source: Subsequent immunisation with recombinant NACHOs boosted the NACHO-specific IgG titers in day 42 serum samples.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: Serum samples from the ferrets that had been re-inoculated with H1N2 reassortant carrying NA derived from A/Stockholm/15/2014 or A/Estonia/91621/2015 showed no further increase in titers, presumably because prior exposure with the same H1N2 virus had induced a sterilising immune response.
source: In contrast, serum samples from the ferrets that had been re-inoculated with H1N2 reassortant carrying NA derived from A/Stockholm/15/2014 or A/Estonia/91621/2015 showed no further increase in titers, presumably because prior exposure with the same H1N2 virus had induced a sterilising immune response (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with speculative interpretation about the mechanism, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Groups of five mice were immunised two times, with a 2-week interval, by intramuscular injection with 1 µg of the respective 43 NACHOs adjuvanted with AF03.
source: Groups of five mice were immunised two times, with a 2-week interval, by intramuscular injection with 1 µg of the respective 43 NACHOs adjuvanted with AF03.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Blood was collected from the immunised mice and serum prepared on day 28 after the prime immunisation.
source: Blood was collected from the immunised mice and serum prepared on day 28 after the prime immunisation (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol, with reference to Figure 1c.

claim: NACHO-specific IgG titers in the mouse immune sera, pooled from each group, ranged from 1:8100 to 1:72,900.
source: NACHO-specific IgG titers in the mouse immune sera, pooled from each group, ranged from 1:8100 to 1:72,900 (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, with reference to Figure 1d.

claim: 27 H6N2 influenza viruses were generated with H6 HA derived from A/mallard/Sweden/2002 and NA derived from a subset of the 43 H3N2 viruses.
source: We generated 27 H6N2 influenza viruses with H6 HA derived from A/mallard/Sweden/2002 and NA derived from a subset of the 43 H3N2 viruses, thereby retaining NA sequence diversity and year of H3N2 virus isolation (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: The 43 NAs used as antigens and 27 NAs as source of NA could be classified into four groups when ordered according to the phylogenetic relatedness of their NA sequence.
source: The 43 NAs used as antigens and 27 NAs as source of NA could be classified into four groups when ordered according to the phylogenetic relatedness of their NA sequence (Figure 2; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from phylogenetic analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The KM of H6N2 viruses ranged from 20.7 to 144.8 µM as determined by the Michaelis-Menten equation.
source: The conversion rate of MUNANA into 4-methylumbelliferyl and acetylneuraminic acid by these H6N2 viruses revealed a KM that ranged from 20.7 to 144.8 µM as determined by the Michaelis-Menten equation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from enzymatic assays, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The KM differs between the distinct phylogenetic groups.
source: Interestingly, the KM differs between the distinct phylogenetic groups (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: There was a negative correlation between the KM values and the dilution of the H6N2 viruses required to set the 70% maximal NA activity in ELLA.
source: There was a negative correlation between the KM values and the dilution of the H6N2 viruses required to set the 70% maximal NA activity in ELLA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: In general, the NAI titers of the ferret sera were the highest against homologous and phylogenetically closely related H6N2 viruses.
source: In general, the NAI titers of the ferret sera were the highest against homologous and phylogenetically closely related H6N2 viruses.
evidence: This is a general observation from the NAI experimental data.

claim: UPGMA-based clustering allowed to discern at least four major antigenic clusters (AC1 to –4).
source: Next, these normalised NAI values were clustered against each of the H6N2s using the unweighted pair group method with arithmetic mean (UPGMA), which is a distance-based method. This clustering allowed to discern at least four major antigenic clusters (AC1 to –4) that are depicted at the top of the heatmap (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from clustering analysis of NAI data, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The H6N2 viruses with NA antigens derived from A/Wisconsin/16/15 and A/Alaska/251/15 do not segregate into AC2, as would be predicted based on the phylogenetic relatedness, but cluster in AC1 based on the UPGMA.
source: It is interesting to note that the H6N2 viruses with NA antigens derived from A/Wisconsin/16/15 and A/Alaska/251/15 do not segregate into AC2, as would be predicted based on the phylogenetic relatedness, but cluster in AC1 based on the UPGMA.
evidence: This is an observation from the clustering analysis showing discordance between phylogenetic and antigenic grouping.

claim: The overall concordance of the antigenicity with the phylogenetic relatedness, based on the amino acid sequences of the NA head domains, was confirmed by hierarchical clustering with bootstrapping and k-means.
source: However, the overall concordance of the antigenicity with the phylogenetic relatedness, based on the amino acid sequences of the NA head domains, was confirmed by hierarchical clustering with bootstrapping and k-means (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple clustering analyses, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: Antigenic cartography analysis resulted in an antigenic map of the N2 NAs that was in line with the four proposed antigenic clusters.
source: In addition, antigenic cartography analysis, based on the method described by Smith et al., 2004, resulted in an antigenic map of the N2 NAs that was in line with the four proposed antigenic clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from antigenic cartography analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citation to Smith et al., 2004.

claim: A positive correlation was observed between the pairwise phylogenetic distances and the normalised NAI IC50 values for each of the tested H6N2s.
source: In line with this, a positive correlation was observed between the pairwise phylogenetic distances and the normalised NAI IC50 values for each of the tested H6N2s (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The normalised data from ferret sera after prime infection confirmed the antigenic clustering observed in sera after boost.
source: The normalised data confirmed the antigenic clustering observed in sera after boost (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from NAI analysis of prime sera, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The mouse NACHO immune sera displayed a similar recognition pattern as the ferret immune sera that had been generated by H1N2 priming followed by a NACHO boost.
source: UPGMA-based clustering showed that the mouse NACHO immune sera displayed a similar recognition pattern as the ferret immune sera that had been generated by H1N2 priming followed by a NACHO boost (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of mouse and ferret sera, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The normalised NAI IC50 values of the ferret and mouse immune sera correlated very well with coefficients values ranging from 0.33 to 0.78.
source: Overall, the normalised NAI IC50 values of the ferret and mouse immune sera correlated very well with coefficients values ranging from 0.33 to 0.78 (Figure 2—figure supplement 6b).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 6b.

claim: NA of human influenza viruses is subject to antigenic drift, predominantly driven by the NAI activity that is detectable in the host serum.
source: NA of human influenza viruses is subject to antigenic drift, predominantly driven by the NAI activity that is detectable in the host serum (Air et al., 1985; Yasuhara et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Air et al., 1985; Yasuhara et al., 2019.

claim: There are a total of 102 amino acid differences between the head domains of the NAs that were used to generate the 43 ferret immune sera.
source: There are a total of 102 amino acid differences between the head domains of the NAs that were used to generate the 43 ferret immune sera (Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: No obvious antigenic patches could be distinguished on the N2 NA surface when significance values higher than 1.3 (p<0.05) were represented on the surface of N2.
source: The significance values higher than 1.3 (p<0.05) of representative strains of the four antigenic groups were represented on the surface of N2 (Figure 3b). No obvious antigenic patches, however, could be distinguished on the N2 NA surface.
evidence: This is a finding from the association analysis and structural mapping, with reference to Figure 3b.

claim: The calculated p-values obtained from the mouse and ferret NAI data were in line with each other in the association analysis.
source: A similar association analysis was performed using the NAI values obtained with the mouse NACHO immune sera. The calculated p-values obtained from the mouse and ferret NAI data were in line with each other (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative association analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Tau values revealed a geometrical distribution with the negative correlations being in closer proximity to the catalytic pocket when visualised on the N2 surface structure.
source: When visualised on the N2 surface structure, the Tau values revealed a geometrical distribution with the negative correlations being in closer proximity to the catalytic pocket (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis and structural mapping, with reference to Figure 4b.

claim: Similar data was obtained when mice sera were analysed for correlation between distances and significance values.
source: Similar data was obtained when mice sera were analysed this way (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from analysis of mouse sera, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The optimised random forest model was built using a combination of 25 randomly sampled features in 1500 decision trees.
source: Here, the optimised model was built using a combination of 25 randomly sampled features in 1500 decision trees.
evidence: This describes the machine learning methodology used in the study.

claim: The random forest model generates predictive antigenic distances that strongly correlate with the observed values with a root-mean-square error (RMSE)/mean = 0.207.
source: The resulting model generates predictive antigenic distances that strongly correlate with the observed values (Figure 5a), with a root-mean-square error (RMSE)/mean = 0.207.
evidence: This is a finding from the machine learning model evaluation, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: The random forest importance scores highlighted similar positions as previously determined in the association study.
source: Those importance scores were represented in a multi-way plot (Figure 5b). The importance scores highlighted similar positions as previously determined in the association study.
evidence: This is a finding from the random forest analysis, with reference to Figure 5b.

claim: The random forest clearly reproduced the drift observed in AC2 versus AC1.
source: The RF clearly reproduced the drift observed in AC2 versus AC1.
evidence: This is a finding from the random forest model predictions.

claim: The modelling indicates that the antigenic distance of the three recent N2s to their corresponding group 2 NAs is increasing whereas their distance to group 4 NAs is decreasing.
source: The modelling also indicates that the antigenic distance of the three recent N2s to their corresponding group 2 NAs is increasing (represented by the dark blue turning light blue, from the A/Singapore/infimh-16-0019/2016 towards the A/Darwin/6/2021 in G2) whereas their distance to group 4 NAs is decreasing (dark red becoming yellow from the A/Singapore/infimh-16-0019/2016 towards the A/Darwin/6/2021 in G4).
evidence: This is a prediction from the random forest model about recent N2 antigenic evolution.

claim: Group 1 contains 22 N2 NAs, 4 of which were derived from vaccine recommended H3N2 strains: A/Perth/16/2009, A/Texas/50/2012, A/Switzerland/9715293/2013, and A/Hong Kong/4801/2014.
source: Group 1 contains 22 N2 NAs, 4 of which were derived from vaccine recommended H3N2 strains: A/Perth/16/2009, A/Texas/50/2012, A/Switzerland/9715293/2013, and A/Hong Kong/4801/2014.
evidence: This describes the composition of phylogenetic group 1 in the study panel.

claim: Phylogenetic group 2 comprises 14 N2 NAs, 1 of which is derived from a vaccine H3N2 recommended strain: A/Singapore/INFIMH-16-0019/2016.
source: Phylogenetic group 2 comprises 14 N2 NAs, 1 of which is derived from a vaccine H3N2 recommended strain: A/Singapore/INFIMH-16-0019/2016.
evidence: This describes the composition of phylogenetic group 2 in the study panel.

claim: The third phylogenetic group contains two NAs that are derived from H3N2 strains that had been isolated in Helsinki in 2013.
source: The third phylogenetic group contains two NAs that are derived from H3N2 strains that had been isolated in Helsinki in 2013.
evidence: This describes the composition of phylogenetic group 3 in the study panel.

claim: The NA sequence of the two Helsinki 2013 strains is closely related to that of H3N2s that circulated more than 15 years earlier (e.g. 99% identity with NA of A/Sydney/5/1997).
source: Remarkably, the NA sequence of these two strains is closely related to that of H3N2s that circulated more than 15 years earlier (e.g. 99% identity with NA of A/Sydney/5/1997).
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis.

claim: The fourth phylogenetic group is composed of NAs derived from zoonotic cases with swine H3N2 strains isolated between 2012 and 2017.
source: The fourth phylogenetic group is composed of NAs derived from zoonotic cases with swine H3N2 strains isolated between 2012 and 2017.
evidence: This describes the composition of phylogenetic group 4 in the study panel.

claim: Swine-to-human transmission of H3N2 viruses have occurred multiple times in the USA in 2012 and continue to be detected at low frequency until to date.
source: Swine-to-human transmission of H3N2 viruses have occurred multiple times in the USA in 2012 and continue to be detected at low frequency until to date (CDC, 2023; Elbe and Buckland-Merrett, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to CDC, 2023; Elbe and Buckland-Merrett, 2017.

claim: Most of the ferrets had detectable serum anti-N2 antibodies by day 14 after infection with H1N2.
source: Most of the ferrets had detectable serum anti-N2 antibodies by day 14 after infection with H1N2.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: Anti-NA antibody titers increased after a boost with non-adjuvanted homologous recombinant CHO-produced soluble tetrameric NA suggesting that the use of recombinant NA may boost naturally acquired anti-NA antibody responses in the human population.
source: Anti-NA antibody titers increased after a boost with non-adjuvanted homologous recombinant CHO-produced soluble tetrameric NA suggesting that the use of recombinant NA may boost naturally acquired anti-NA antibody responses in the human population.
evidence: This is an experimental finding with speculative extrapolation to human populations.

claim: The NAI activity of the ferret sera against 27 tested H6N2s reassortants revealed a pattern of inhibition that largely coincides with the phylogenetic distances based on the NA head domain sequences.
source: The NAI activity of the ferret sera against 27 tested H6N2s reassortants revealed a pattern of inhibition that largely coincides with the phylogenetic distances based on the NA head domain sequences.
evidence: This is a finding from the NAI analysis.

claim: H6N2 with Kan17 NA had a broader profile of inhibition than other H6N2 viruses from group 2, being also inhibited by serum raised against NA from phylogenetic groups 3 and, to a lesser extent, group 4.
source: We noted that H6N2 with Kan17 NA had a broader profile of inhibition than other H6N2 viruses from group 2, being also inhibited by serum raised against NA from phylogenetic groups 3 and, to a lesser extent, group 4.
evidence: This is an observation from the NAI data.

claim: The H6N2s Wis15 and Ala15 have an antigenic behaviour that is more closely related to antigenic cluster 1, despite belonging to group 2 according to their phylogenetic similarities.
source: Additionally, the H6N2s Wis15 and Ala15 have an antigenic behaviour that is more closely related to antigenic cluster 1, despite belonging to group 2 according to their phylogenetic similarities.
evidence: This is an observation from the NAI data showing discordance between phylogenetic and antigenic grouping.

claim: The amino acid substitutions S245N and S247T, combined with substitution P468H, were identified in the association analysis and were described as major contributors of the NA antigenic drift that occurred in H3N2 in 2014.
source: It is interesting to note that the amino acid substitutions S245N and S247T, combined with substitution P468H, were identified in this association analysis. Those substitutions were described as major contributors of the NA antigenic drift that occurred in H3N2 in 2014 (Wan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the association analysis, supported by citation to Wan et al., 2019.

claim: NAs from A/Wisconsin/16/2015 and A/Alaska/251/2015 have the S245N and S247T substitutions but lack the P468H mutation and are antigenically closer to group 1 NAs, confirming the requirement of P468H combined with the S245N and S247T substitutions for this NA antigenic drift.
source: NAs from A/Wisconsin/16/2015 and A/Alaska/251/2015 also have the S245N and S247T substitutions and phylogenetically belong to group 2 NAs. However, those 2 NAs lack the P468H mutation and are antigenically closer to group 1 NAs, confirming the requirement of P468H combined with the S245N and S247T substitutions for this NA antigenic drift (Wan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from the study that confirms a previous observation, with citation to Wan et al., 2019.

claim: NA antigenic drift may sometimes require a combination of amino acid changes rather than single mutations.
source: This observation suggests that NA antigenic drift may sometimes require a combination of amino acid changes rather than single mutations.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about the S245N, S247T, and P468H substitutions.

claim: N2 antigenic evolution is constrained by charge balances in an antigenic region, which can partially explain the observation that NA amino acids can undergo co-evolution to result in antigenic drift.
source: Wang and colleagues have very elegantly demonstrated that N2 antigenic evolution is constrained by charge balances in an antigenic region, which can partially explain the observation that NA amino acids can undergo co-evolution to result in antigenic drift (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: NAs originated from H3N2 variants classified in phylogenetic group 4 were antigenically closer to N2s belonging to phylogenetic group 1.
source: Interestingly, NAs originated from H3N2 variants classified in phylogenetic group 4 were antigenically closer to N2s belonging to phylogenetic group 1.
evidence: This is a finding from the antigenic analysis.

claim: The antigenic drift of recent NAs from group 2 increases the antigenic distance from the N2s of swine origin.
source: This suggest that the antigenic drift of recent NAs from group 2 increases the antigenic distance from the N2s of swine origin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation about group 4 NAs being antigenically closer to group 1.

claim: The analysis of the sera obtained from ferrets after infection shows that the inhibition pattern evaluated against five distinct H6N2s is in accordance with the response obtained after boosting with recombinant protein, despite the lower homologous anti-NA titers.
source: Noteworthy, the analysis of the sera obtained from ferrets after infection shows that, despite the lower homologous anti-NA titers, the inhibition pattern evaluated against five distinct H6N2s (composed of at least one representative of each antigenic group) is in accordance with the response obtained after boosting with recombinant protein.
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of prime and boost sera.

claim: A boost with homologous recombinant soluble tetrameric NA does not alter the breadth of the antibody response induced by H1N2 infection only.
source: This suggests that a boost with homologous recombinant soluble tetrameric NA does not alter the breadth of the antibody response induced by H1N2 infection only.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of prime and boost sera patterns.

claim: Repeated H3N2 virus exposure of ferrets affects anti-HA responses.
source: It has been reported that repeated H3N2 virus exposure of ferrets affects anti-HA responses (Kosikova et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kosikova et al., 2018.

claim: Studies in mice can offer a convenient alternative to the use of ferrets in future NA antigenicity studies.
source: Studies in mice can thus offer a convenient alternative to the use of ferrets in future NA antigenicity studies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that mouse and ferret sera showed similar NAI patterns.

claim: There may be universal rules of immunogen antigenicity and immunogenicity.
source: This data also supports the hypothesis that there may be universal rules of immunogen antigenicity and immunogenicity (Altman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Altman et al., 2015.

claim: The KM values of the H6N2 viruses indicate that substrate affinity tends to vary according to the phylogenetic relatedness of N2s.
source: The determined KM values of the H6N2 viruses used here indicate that substrate affinity tends to vary according to the phylogenetic relatedness of N2s.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the KM measurements.

claim: The N-glycosylation at position 245 was previously described to be responsible for reducing N2 affinity for its substrate.
source: The N-glycosylation at position 245 was previously described to be responsible for reducing N2 affinity for its substrate (Powell and Pekosz, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Powell and Pekosz, 2020.

claim: NAs from phylogenetic group 4 have a low KM, indicating an increased affinity for substrate, unlike group 2 which is primarily characterised by the presence of an N-glycan at position 245.
source: Unlike group 2, which is primarily characterised by the presence of an N-glycan at position 245, NAs from phylogenetic group 4 have a low KM, indicating an increased affinity for substrate.
evidence: This is a finding from the KM measurements.

claim: Phylogenetic drift can be accompanied by changes in NA enzymatic properties.
source: This result suggests that phylogenetic drift can be accompanied by changes in NA enzymatic properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that KM varies by phylogenetic group.

claim: The Ala15, Wis15, and Kan17 H6N2s, despite having antigenic properties closer to group 1, still have KM values that are comparable to those of group 2 N2 NAs.
source: Curiously, the Ala15, Wis15, and Kan17, despite having antigenic properties closer to group 1, still have KM values that are comparable to those of group 2 N2 NAs.
evidence: This is an observation from the KM measurements showing discordance between antigenic and enzymatic properties.

claim: The training dataset for the random forest model was based on the 102 mutations present in the panel, limiting the predictions for other positions.
source: However, it is important to note that the training dataset was based on the 102 mutations present in our panel, limiting the predictions for other positions.
evidence: This is a limitation of the machine learning approach acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The random forest modelling does not consider that substitution by other amino acids can have a distinct impact on the antigenic distance.
source: Furthermore, RF enabled the classification of the variable amino acids according to importance scores. Also, our modelling does not consider that substitution by other amino acids can have a distinct impact on the antigenic distance.
evidence: This is a limitation of the machine learning approach acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Predictions based on the random forest model could underestimate the importance of a particular amino acid residue substitution in some cases.
source: As a consequence, predictions based on the model could underestimate the importance of a particular amino acid residue substitution in some cases.
evidence: This is a limitation of the machine learning approach acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Co-occurring substitutions in the panel (the ones present in the main branches of the phylogenetic tree) cannot be individually assessed by association analysis or the RF model.
source: It is important to highlight that co-occurring substitutions in our panel (the ones present in the main branches of the phylogenetic tree) cannot be individually assessed by association analysis or the RF model.
evidence: This is a limitation of the analytical approaches acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The individual weight of co-occurring mutations on NA drift remains to be experimentally demonstrated.
source: The individual weight of those mutation on NA drift thus remains to be experimentally demonstrated.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The modelling could put in evidence the gradual drift of recent N2s which were not present in the dataset (A/Hong Kong/45/2019, A/Tasmania/503/2020, and A/Darwin/6/2021).
source: Interestingly, the modelling could put in evidence the gradual drift of recent N2s which were not present in the dataset (A/Hong Kong/45/2019, A/Tasmania/503/2020, and A/Darwin/6/2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the predictive modeling.

claim: An N-glycosylation site at position 329 combined with E344 in NA from human H3N2 viruses from 2007 to 2013 was gradually lost in later H3N2 viruses.
source: It has been reported that an N-glycosylation site at position 329 combined with E344 in NA from human H3N2 viruses from 2007 to 2013 was gradually lost in later H3N2 viruses (Ge et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ge et al., 2022.

claim: The loss of an N-glycosylation site at position 329 combined with an E344K substitution was associated with a change in NAI reactivity in ferret sera.
source: This loss of an N-glycosylation site at position 329 combined with an E344K substitution was associated with a change in NAI reactivity in ferret sera.
evidence: This is a statement about a previously reported finding.

claim: Three N2 NAs in the panel, derived from A/Victoria/361/2011, A/Hong_Kong/3089/2017, and A/Tennessee/18/2017, lack the N-glycosylation motif at position 329.
source: Three N2 NAs in our panel, derived from A/Victoria/361/2011, A/Hong_Kong/3089/2017, and A/Tennessee/18/2017, lack this N-glycosylation motif.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis of the study panel.

claim: The E344K substitution is present in three NAs, derived from A/Nagano/2153/2017, A/Minnesota/11/2010, and A/Indiana/08/2011.
source: The E344K substitution is present in three other NAs, derived from A/Nagano/2153/2017, A/Minnesota/11/2010, and A/Indiana/08/2011.
evidence: This is a finding from sequence analysis of the study panel.

claim: The importance of the E344K and position 329 N-glycosylation mutations is among the lowest ones predicted by the random forest modelling.
source: The importance of those mutations is among the lowest ones predicted by our modelling.
evidence: This is a finding from the random forest analysis.

claim: The differences in NAI reported by Ge et al. for the E344K and position 329 N-glycosylation mutations are very modest (less than twofold).
source: However, the differences in NAI reported by Ge et al. are very modest (less than twofold).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a previous study.

claim: The experimental variability in the study potentially limits the identification of substitutions with a subtle impact on NAI.
source: The experimental variability in our study potentially limits the identification of substitutions with a subtle impact on NAI.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study.

claim: The protective potential of NA antigen against influenza has been underscored by multiple studies.
source: The protective potential of NA antigen against influenza has been underscored by multiple studies.
evidence: This is a statement about established knowledge in the field.

claim: NA will likely be included as a standard component of next-generation influenza vaccines.
source: It is likely that NA will be included as a standard component of next-generation influenza vaccines.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future vaccine development.

claim: The difficulties of producing stable tetrameric NA may be overcome in the future, thanks to protein design or with the advent of mRNA-based vaccines.
source: The difficulties of producing stable tetrameric NA may be overcome in the future, thanks to protein design or with the advent of mRNA-based vaccines (Catani et al., 2022; Chivukula et al., 2021; Ellis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future vaccine development, supported by citations to Catani et al., 2022; Chivukula et al., 2021; Ellis et al., 2022.

claim: The antigenic modelling associated with sequence surveillance may increase predictive ability, highlighting major potential drifts and support NA antigen designs that may elicit broader NAI responses compared to natural NA.
source: The antigenic modelling associated with sequence surveillance may increase our predictive ability, highlighting major potential drifts and support NA antigen designs that may elicit broader NAI responses compared to natural NA.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications of the study findings.

claim: Immunisation with recombinant N2 NA immunogen can boost anti-NA serum antibody responses in ferrets that were primed by infection with an influenza virus that carries the homologous NA.
source: In summary, our study shows that immunisation with recombinant N2 NA immunogen can boost anti-NA serum antibody responses in ferrets that were primed by infection with an influenza virus that carries the homologous NA.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: The four major antigenic groups distinguished in N2 NA predominantly correspond with the phylogenetic relatedness of the N2 head domains.
source: At least four major antigenic groups could be distinguished in N2 NA derived from human H3N2 viruses that were isolated between 2009 and 2017, and those antigenic groups predominantly correspond with the phylogenetic relatedness of the N2 head domains.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.

claim: The amino acid substitutions in close proximity of the NA catalytic pocket are more likely to affect NAI patterns.
source: In addition, the amino acid substitutions in close proximity of the NA catalytic pocket are more likely to affect NAI patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding from the study.
